headline: Technology Vendors Learned What Saudi Contractors Will Actually Buy
deck: Pitches built on artificial intelligence got short hearings at Big 5. Pitches built on a task, a cycle time and a reference project got meetings.
excerpt: Construction technology vendors at Big 5 Construct Saudi found a market willing to buy and unwilling to be impressed. Robotics and sensing pitches that named a task, a measurable result and a reference project outperformed platform and AI positioning.
content:
Technology vendors had the hardest four days of anyone at Big 5 Construct Saudi, and the reason was not hostility. Saudi contractors walked their stands willing to buy and unwilling to be impressed, and the vendors who understood the difference did well.

The pattern across conversations was consistent. A vendor leading with artificial intelligence, digital transformation or a connected platform got a polite hearing and a short one. A vendor leading with a task, a cycle time and a reference project got a technical discussion and often a follow-up meeting. The distinction is not about sophistication. It is about which claim a contractor can test before signing.

Construction is unusually well defended against technology selling because it has been sold to before. The industry absorbed a decade of software that promised coordination and delivered another system for a site engineer to update, and the memory of that is priced into every conversation. What has changed is that a category of construction technology now produces physically observable results, and contractors can tell the difference.

Robotics is the clearest example. The compelling applications on the floor were narrow and repetitive: spraying, plastering, sanding and finishing, grinding, trenching, reinforcement processing, and inspection. DaFang AI, a Shenzhen manufacturer of building-surface robots, sells machines built to exactly that shape. Its DF033 unit combines putty plastering, fine sanding and latex paint spraying to a height of 3.3 metres in rooms too narrow for scaffolded crews; a larger DF062 works to six metres with dynamic obstacle avoidance. The company's DF061 model has been used on public housing work in Hong Kong's Tuen Mun, where it was reported to cut construction time on that scope by roughly a tenth. Whether or not a Saudi contractor accepts that figure, it is the right kind of claim: bounded, attributable and checkable.

Sensing is the second category that survived scrutiny. Connected concrete was among the more striking things on show, because concrete is the least digital material in the industry and is becoming a measurable one. Brickeye, formerly AOMS Technologies, sells wireless sensors that report internal concrete temperature, temperature differential and maturity in real time under its LumiCon product, letting a site strike formwork on measured strength rather than a calendar assumption, and flagging thermal cracking risk in mass pours before it becomes a failed element. The company says its technology has been deployed on more than 3,000 projects across more than 20 countries.

What both examples share is that they replace a judgement with a measurement, and the measurement maps directly onto a cost the contractor already carries: a delayed pour, a rejected element, a crew waiting on a wall. BrentDesk's reporting on the physical economy becoming a technology market describes the same pattern across heavy industry, and construction is a late but genuine participant in it.

Capital cost is the constraint vendors most often under-addressed. Industry surveys put purpose-built construction robots in a band from roughly $100,000 to $500,000 and above per unit, which for a Saudi contractor means the machine must be deployable across many projects rather than one, and must have a service and spares presence in the Kingdom. Specialist subcontractors with repeatable scopes across a portfolio are the natural first buyers, not general contractors, and the vendors who had worked that out were pitching to the right people.

The second under-addressed issue was integration. Contractors asked, repeatedly, what a system does after it detects something. An alert that arrives in a proprietary dashboard nobody logs into is an expense. The vendors making progress were those who could describe how their output reaches a work order, a procurement decision or a foreman's phone, which is the same closed-loop problem the industrial world has been working through.

The third was proof in this market. A reference from a European or East Asian project is a starting point in Riyadh, not a conclusion, because Saudi sites differ in ambient temperature, crew composition, supervision structure and inspection regime. Several vendors arrived looking for a first Saudi deployment they could point to, which is a reasonable objective for a show and a more honest one than claiming a track record they do not yet have.

The market at Riyadh Front was not resistant to technology. It was resistant to unfalsifiable claims, and it was buying from anyone who turned up with a number.
author: Mo Qureshi
seoTitle: What Saudi Contractors Will Actually Buy From Tech Vendors
